title: Japan Comes Last in Global Workplace Happiness
paragraphs: What makes people happy at work? Is it being interested in what they do? Having friendly colleagues? Feeling that their boss values them?

A new international survey has looked at how happy people are at work. The survey, by French employee benefits company Edenred, asked about 26,000 people in 27 countries about their experiences at work.
It looked at things like people's relationships with colleagues, their feelings about their jobs, and whether they felt valued for what they did to find their "joy score."
The average "joy score" for all 27 countries was 63 out of 100.
India had the highest score, at 73. Mexico and Peru were close behind, with 72 points each.
But Japan came last, with just 47 points out of 100. In fact, more than half of the Japanese workers in the survey fell into the "low joy" group.
The survey also found that 40% of Japan's human resources managers believed that worker engagement had improved over the last year — but only 10% of workers said they actually felt more engaged.
Around the world, 94% of workers in the "high joy" group said they expected to stay with their company the next year. For the "low joy" group, it was 63%.
This doesn't mean that happiness makes people stay in their jobs. But the two seem to be connected.
So what helps people feel happier at work?
The survey found that workers who received recognition or praise from their bosses were more likely to want to stay with their company.
So for companies that want to keep their workers, saying "thank you" for a job well done could be a good place to start!
